lessons.title: Anglo-Saxon crime, communities and the wergild
lessons.description: How village communities, tithings and the hue and cry kept order before 1066.
lessons.content_html:
A Society Without Police

Late Anglo-Saxon England, around the year 1000, was a small farming society of perhaps two million people. There were no police, no prisons in the modern sense, and no professional courts. Yet villages still needed to keep order — theft of livestock, violent quarrels and disputes over land could not be ignored. The kings of Wessex and Mercia, including King Æthelstan, set out written law codes to defend what was called the king’s peace. The system depended on neighbours watching neighbours: order came from the community, not from the state.

Crimes fell into three broad groups. Crimes against the person included assault and murder. Crimes against property covered theft and arson. Crimes against authority included treason against the king and refusal to pay taxes. The most serious offences — treason and murder — were punished by death, but most everyday disputes were settled with fines and compensation rather than execution.

Key Fact

Anglo-Saxon law recognised three categories of crime: against the person (assault, murder), against property (theft, arson) and against authority (treason, tax evasion). The king’s peace covered all of them.

Tithings and Collective Responsibility

Every free man over the age of twelve belonged to a tithing — a group of ten men who were collectively responsible for each other’s behaviour. If one member of the tithing committed a crime, the others had to bring him to court or pay a heavy fine themselves. This was known as collective responsibility, and it forced communities to police themselves.

When a crime was witnessed, anyone could raise the hue and cry. Every man in the village was legally obliged to drop his work and chase the suspected criminal. Failure to join the chase meant the whole village could be fined. Above the village, the shire reeve — the origin of the modern word ‘sheriff’ — collected fines and presided over the shire court on behalf of the king.

It is tempting to describe the hue and cry as if it were a uniform, nationwide police force. It was not. Whether the chase was successful depended entirely on the local community — how alert neighbours were, whether they were willing to abandon their work, and whether the criminal had local support. In tightly knit villages it could be effective; in towns or along busy roads it was often easily evaded. Examiners reward students who treat the hue and cry as a community-driven system that varied in effectiveness, not as a national police force.

Trial by Jury and Oath-Helping

Once a suspect was caught, the case went to a local court. There were no professional lawyers. Instead, the accused was tried by a jury of local men who already knew them. A central feature was oath-helping: the accused gathered ‘oath-helpers’ who swore in court that the accused was telling the truth. The more respected the oath-helpers, the stronger the defence. This was a system based on personal reputation, not on physical evidence as we would understand it today. If a verdict could not be reached, more dramatic methods such as trial by ordeal could follow — a topic for a later lesson.

Wergild: Compensation, Not Just Punishment

If someone was killed or injured, the wrongdoer often had to pay wergild, literally ‘man-price’. This compensation was paid not to the king but to the victim or the victim’s family. The amount depended on the social rank of the victim. By the laws of King Cnut, the death of a nobleman could cost roughly 1,200 shillings; a free peasant’s life was valued at around 200 shillings; a slave’s, less still. Even injuries had a price — loss of an ear, a finger or an eye each had a fixed payment.

The point of wergild was to head off the blood feud. Without compensation, an injured family might take revenge by killing the offender, which would trigger another revenge killing in return. Wergild allowed a wrong to be settled in cash and stopped feuds from escalating. It is therefore a mistake to read Anglo-Saxon punishment as simply brutal: it combined harsh penalties for serious crime with a pragmatic system of restitution that kept communities together.

A common error is to describe wergild as a fine paid to the king or to the courts. It was not. It was compensation paid directly to the victim or, if the victim had been killed, to their surviving family. Fines paid to the king (called the wite) did exist alongside wergild and were sometimes added on top, but the wergild itself was a private payment that recognised the victim’s loss. Treating it as a private compensation, not a state fine, is what unlocks the higher mark band.

Deterrence and Retribution

For serious crimes that were not settled by wergild, Anglo-Saxon punishment was deliberately public and harsh. Corporal punishments included branding, flogging and the cutting off of a hand for repeated theft. Capital punishments — hanging or beheading — were reserved for treason, arson and the worst murders. Under Edward the Confessor, the law continued to mix money compensation, mutilation and execution depending on the nature of the offence and the rank of the victim.

Two ideas guided this system. The first was deterrence: punishments were carried out in the open so that other villagers would think twice before offending. The second was retribution — the idea that a wrong done to a person or community had to be visibly answered. Neither idea was about reforming the criminal, an aim that would only emerge centuries later. In a small farming society where survival depended on neighbours trusting one another, the priority was to restore order quickly and clearly.

Key Fact

Wergild was paid to the victim or the victim’s family, not to the king. By providing compensation for death or injury it was designed to prevent the blood feud, in which families took revenge through more killings.

lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Anglo-Saxon law enforcement was community-based: tithings of ten men shared collective responsibility, and the hue and cry obliged every villager to chase suspected criminals.
  • Wergild was compensation paid to the victim’s family, scaled by social rank, and existed mainly to prevent blood feuds — punishment was therefore both restorative and retributive, not just brutal.
  • Above the village, the shire reeve enforced the king’s peace and presided over shire courts; corporal and capital punishments were reserved for the most serious offences against person, property and authority.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Anglo-Saxons relied on the local community to enforce the law.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for an explanation of two or more reasons, supported by accurate detail from the period.

Indicative content:
• There were no professional police, courts or prisons; the king did not have the resources to enforce law in every village.
• Anglo-Saxon society was small, rural and tightly knit — neighbours knew one another and could identify wrongdoers quickly.
• The system of tithings shared responsibility across ten men, so the whole group had a financial incentive to keep their members honest.
• The hue and cry mobilised the whole village against a criminal at no cost to the king.
• Compensation through wergild meant disputes could be settled locally, reducing the need for royal intervention.

Mastering: Sustained explanation of at least two reasons, each developed with specific period detail (e.g. tithing, hue and cry, wergild) and explicit links to the question.
Secure: Two reasons clearly explained with relevant detail; links to the question are present but less developed.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of features without explaining why the community had this role.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Anglo-Saxon wergild system.

• Specific injuries had fixed payments — for example loss of a finger, ear or eye each had a set price.
• It was designed to prevent the blood feud by giving the victim's family a settled payment instead of revenge.

practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement (with SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 16 marks for the historical content, plus up to 4 SPaG marks for accuracy and use of period-specific vocabulary.

Indicative content — arguments supporting deterrence as the main purpose:
• Corporal punishments such as flogging, branding and the cutting off of a hand were carried out in public so that other villagers would think twice before offending.
• Capital punishment for treason, arson and the worst murders sent a clear public message that some crimes would cost the offender their life.
• The hue and cry made it likely that a criminal would be caught quickly, raising the perceived cost of breaking the law.

Indicative content — arguments against (other purposes):
• Wergild was about restitution rather than deterrence — it compensated the victim's family and headed off the blood feud, restoring relationships in the community.
• Tithings emphasised collective responsibility, which is closer to prevention than to deterrence after the fact.
• Retribution — the visible answer to a wrong done — was at least as central as deterrence; the law was deeply concerned with social rank and balance.
• Reform of the offender was not yet an aim, but maintaining communal harmony was.

Mastering: Sustained, well-supported argument that weighs deterrence against at least one other purpose, uses accurate period vocabulary, and reaches a clear, justified judgement signposted in the introduction and conclusion.
Secure: Both sides considered with relevant detail; judgement is present but less consistently developed.
Developing: One side developed more than the other; judgement is asserted rather than defended.
Emerging: Limited argument with little period detail; no clear judgement.

SPaG (4 marks): Accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar with consistent use of subject-specific historical terminology (e.g. tithing, wergild, shire reeve, hue and cry, retribution).

practice_questions.text: Explain why the wergild was important in Anglo-Saxon society.
practice_questions.marks:

lessons.title: The Norman Conquest and William's Forest Laws
lessons.description: How 1066 changed crime: new Forest Laws, Murdrum and Norman royal authority.
lessons.content_html:
A Conqueror Layered on Top of Anglo-Saxon Law

After his victory at Hastings in 1066, William I (the Conqueror) faced a problem familiar to any conqueror: he was a French-speaking ruler imposing himself on roughly two million English-speaking people. Wholesale replacement of English law would have provoked rebellion. Instead William kept much of what he found — the king’s peace, tithings, the hue and cry, the shire reeve and the local courts — and layered Norman additions on top. This is a key idea: the Conquest brought significant change in what counted as a crime, but considerable continuity in how communities still helped to police themselves.

The Norman additions had two purposes. The first was to protect Norman lords, who were a small armed minority in a hostile country. The second was to enrich the king and project his power over land, hunting and movement. Forest Laws, the Murdrum fine and trial by combat all served those aims.

Key Fact

The Norman Conquest is a story of change AND continuity. New crimes (Forest Laws, Murdrum) and a new trial method (trial by combat) were layered on top of an older system that kept tithings, the hue and cry, the shire reeve and local courts.

The Royal Forest and the Forest Laws

From 1071 onwards, William and his sons designated huge areas of woodland and farmland as royal forest. By the reign of Henry I, around a third of England was royal forest. These were not necessarily wooded — whole villages could find themselves enclosed by forest boundaries.

Inside this land the Forest Laws applied. It became a crime to hunt deer or wild boar, to fell trees, to gather firewood, to graze pigs or to own a dog capable of catching game without first having three of its claws cut. Punishments were severe: fines that could ruin a peasant family, mutilation (the loss of fingers, an eye or worse) and, in extreme cases, death.

For an English peasant who had previously gathered wood or hunted small game on what they thought was common land, this was a sudden criminalisation of everyday life. Historians describe such offences — illegal in law but widely accepted by ordinary people — as social crime. Poaching is the textbook example: most villagers helped poachers and refused to inform on them, so the law was widely broken with community approval.

Modern students often dismiss poaching as a small offence. Under Norman Forest Law it was anything but minor. Killing a royal deer could cost an offender a hand, an eye or, in some cases, his life. The change in law — not the change in behaviour — is what created the crime. The same act of hunting that had been ordinary in 1065 could be punished with mutilation in 1075. Examiners reward students who explain that the Conquest changed the legal definition of what counted as crime; the food remained the same, only the laws around it changed.

The Murdrum Fine

In the years immediately after 1066, English resistance to Norman rule sometimes meant the assassination of Norman lords. William responded with the Murdrum fine. If a Norman was found dead in a village or hundred and the killer could not be produced, the entire local community had to pay a heavy collective fine. The fine could be ruinous, and it gave English villagers a strong incentive to identify the murderer themselves rather than shield him.

It is important not to confuse the Murdrum with a general murder law. It applied specifically when the victim was Norman; it did not apply when an Englishman was killed. Like the Forest Laws, it was designed to protect the new ruling class. It also extended the older Anglo-Saxon idea of collective responsibility: the community was now answerable not only for its own members but for any unsolved Norman death within its bounds.

Students often write that the Murdrum fine punished murder in general. It did not. It was a specific tool to protect Normans from English attack. If the killer of a Norman was named and produced for trial, the fine was avoided. If not, the local community paid — whether they had any hand in the killing or not. The point was practical, not moral: it pressured English communities into policing each other on behalf of the new king.

Trial by Combat — A New Way to Decide a Verdict

The Normans also brought trial by combat, in which the accused and accuser fought one another with swords or staves; God was believed to grant victory to the truthful. It supplemented — rather than replaced — the Anglo-Saxon trials by jury and oath-helpers. Trial by ordeal continued too, until the Church withdrew clerical participation in 1215 (the subject of the next lesson). Crucially, the existing tithings, the hue and cry and shire courts continued to function alongside these Norman additions: the village constable still chased criminals, but those criminals could now be charged with offences invented since 1066.

Henry II and the Royal Courts

Almost a century after Hastings, Henry II went further. The Assize of Clarendon (1166) required local juries to report serious offences to royal judges who travelled the country. These judges applied the same rules in every shire, creating what would later be called the common law. The result was that, while Anglo-Saxon community policing remained the day-to-day reality, royal justice now reached deeper into the countryside than it had in 1066. Continuity at the bottom of the system; substantial change at the top.

Key Fact

The Murdrum fine was charged on a whole community when a Norman was found murdered and the killer could not be produced. It was specifically designed to protect Normans, and could be avoided by handing over the killer.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark ‘Explain Why’ on the Norman Conquest, do not write a description of life under William. Pick two clear reasons (for example, protecting the Norman ruling class, and projecting royal authority over land and hunting), explain each with a specific example (Murdrum, Forest Laws), and link the example back to the question. For a 4-mark ‘Consequence’ question, focus tightly on what changed AS A RESULT of 1066 — the criminalisation of poaching is a strong, specific consequence; vague answers about ‘life getting worse’ are capped. Use period vocabulary throughout (Forest Laws, Murdrum, royal forest, social crime, trial by combat) to access the SPaG band.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Conquest brought change AND continuity: tithings, the hue and cry and shire courts continued, while Forest Laws, the Murdrum fine and trial by combat were layered on top.
  • Forest Laws criminalised everyday peasant activities such as gathering wood and hunting; poaching became the classic ‘social crime’ — illegal but supported by the local community.
  • The Murdrum fine specifically protected Normans by punishing whole English communities when a Norman killing went unsolved; under Henry II, royal courts (Assize of Clarendon, 1166) extended royal justice further still.

• It extended the older Anglo-Saxon idea of collective responsibility (already used in tithings) so that the same machinery now policed Anglo-Norman relations.
• The fine reinforced William's wider strategy: keep most Anglo-Saxon law intact, but layer on new measures specifically aimed at securing his rule and protecting his followers.

lessons.title: The Church, sanctuary and trial by ordeal
lessons.description: How the medieval Church shaped crime, sanctuary and the end of trial by ordeal in 1215.
lessons.content_html:
A Parallel Legal System

In medieval England the Church was not just a religious organisation; it was a parallel legal system. It had its own courts, its own punishments and its own laws (canon law). Anyone classed as a clergyman could insist on being tried in Church courts rather than by the king’s courts. Church courts handled offences by priests, monks and nuns, but also moral offences such as adultery and blasphemy that the royal courts often left alone.

The Church courts mattered for one big reason: they could not impose the death penalty. Their punishments were penances — pilgrimage, fasting, public confession — and at the most severe end, life imprisonment in a monastery. For accused criminals the difference between standing trial in a king’s court and a Church court could be the difference between life and death.

Key Fact

Church courts ran in parallel with royal courts in medieval England. They handled cases involving clergy and moral offences, and crucially could not impose capital punishment.

Benefit of Clergy

Benefit of Clergy was the right of a clergyman to be tried in a Church court instead of a royal court. To prove clerical status, the accused had to read aloud Psalm 51 in Latin: “Miserere mei, Deus” — ‘Have mercy on me, O God’. Because Latin literacy was rare and overwhelmingly clerical, this was a reasonable test in the early Middle Ages.

Over time, however, criminals memorised the verse. By the later Middle Ages anyone who could recite the so-called neck verse could claim Benefit of Clergy and escape the death penalty. Hence its nickname: it could literally save your neck. To prevent constant abuse, royal courts began branding successful claimants on the thumb so they could not use the privilege twice.

Students often write that Benefit of Clergy was reserved for ordained priests, monks and nuns. In strict theory it was — but in practice the test (reciting Psalm 51 in Latin) meant anyone literate enough to memorise the verse could claim it. By the late medieval period the privilege had effectively become a benefit of literacy. The royal courts knew this and tried to limit it by branding successful claimants on the thumb, but they could not abolish it — that would require centuries of further reform. Examiners reward students who explain that the loophole was widely exploited rather than describing it as a strict clerical privilege.

Sanctuary

Sanctuary was the right of a fugitive to claim refuge inside a consecrated church. A criminal who reached the church door and grasped the iron knocker (sometimes a special ‘sanctuary ring’) could not be dragged out by the king’s officers. Inside, they had forty days to make a choice. They could surrender themselves and stand trial, or they could swear an oath to leave the kingdom — called abjuring the realm — and walk barefoot to a designated port carrying a wooden cross.

Sanctuary was widely used. Some churches, like Beverley Minster and Durham Cathedral, became famous as sanctuary sites and kept records of those who claimed refuge there. The system reflects the Church’s sense of itself as a separate authority: even a hardened robber, once inside its walls, was protected from the king’s justice for forty days.

Trial by Ordeal

Trial by ordeal was used when local juries could not reach a verdict and the case was particularly serious. The Church played a central role: priests blessed the water, prayed over the iron and pronounced God’s judgement on the result. There were several forms.

In the ordeal of hot iron, the accused carried a red-hot bar nine feet, and the wound was bandaged. Three days later, the bandage was removed: a clean wound meant innocence; a festering wound, guilt. In the ordeal of cold water, the accused was bound and lowered into a blessed pool. If they sank, the holy water had ‘accepted’ them and they were innocent; if they floated, they were guilty. In the ordeal of hot water, the accused plunged a hand into boiling water to retrieve a stone — again, the wound was inspected three days later. Trial by ordeal of blessed bread (the corsned) was reserved mainly for clergy.

From a modern point of view these tests look brutal and irrational. To medieval people they were rational because they assumed God would not let an innocent person suffer. Trial by ordeal was the system’s way of asking God for an answer when human evidence had run out.

1215: The End of Clerical Participation

The decisive shift came in 1215. Pope Innocent III convened the Fourth Lateran Council in Rome. Among its many rulings, the Council forbade clergymen from participating in trial by ordeal. Without a priest to bless the iron or the water, the ordeals could no longer claim God’s judgement — and so they collapsed.

A common error is to say that ordeals ended because people simply stopped believing in them. The decisive event was institutional, not popular: in 1215 the Church — led by Pope Innocent III at the Fourth Lateran Council — forbade clergy from blessing the water, fire or iron. Without clerical participation the result of the ordeal could no longer be read as God’s judgement, and the practice ceased. Belief in divine judgement persisted long after; the change was a top-down institutional decision.

The collapse of trial by ordeal left a gap in serious criminal cases. The royal courts filled it by extending trial by jury — the very system that had handled lighter cases for centuries. Twelve men of the local hundred would now decide guilt or innocence, weighing the evidence themselves rather than waiting for divine signs. This shift, an unintended consequence of a Church reform, is one of the most important moments in the long history of English criminal justice.

Key Fact

In 1215 the Fourth Lateran Council, called by Pope Innocent III, banned clergy from taking part in trial by ordeal. Without priests to pronounce God’s judgement, the practice ended — and royal trial by jury filled the gap.

lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The medieval Church ran a parallel legal system. Church courts could not impose the death penalty, so Benefit of Clergy and sanctuary often saved accused people from hanging.
  • Trial by ordeal — iron, water and hot water — relied on clergy pronouncing God’s judgement; people believed God would protect the innocent.
  • In 1215 the Fourth Lateran Council, called by Pope Innocent III, forbade clergy from participating in ordeals. The practice collapsed and royal trial by jury extended to fill the gap.

lessons.title: Early modern crime: heresy, treason and witchcraft
lessons.description: How vagabondage, heresy and witchcraft became the new crimes of c1500–c1700.
lessons.content_html:
A Period of New Crimes

Between c1500 and c1700, England did not stop punishing the old crimes — theft, assault, murder and treason were still serious offences, still tried in royal courts, and still punished harshly. The framework of tithings, parish constables and royal courts continued. What changed was that whole new categories of crime were created. Religious change made heresy a major capital offence. Economic change criminalised the wandering poor as vagabondage. And from 1542, social anxieties were channelled into the formal prosecution of witchcraft. This lesson examines all three.

Key Fact

Three new crimes defined the early modern period: heresy (Henry VIII’s Reformation onwards), vagabondage (1547 Vagrancy Act, refined by the 1601 Poor Law) and witchcraft (1542 Witchcraft Act).

Heresy and Treason: The Reformation Reshapes Crime

Until the 1530s, English Christianity was Catholic and answered to the Pope in Rome. Henry VIII’s break with Rome (1534) made the king, not the pope, the head of the English Church. From then on, refusing to accept this could be treason as well as heresy — and the line between the two became blurred.

Under Mary I, England returned briefly to Rome. The heresy laws were revived and roughly 280 Protestants were burnt at the stake between 1555 and 1558 — the so-called ‘Protestant martyrs’ whose stories John Foxe later collected in his Book of Martyrs. When Elizabeth I succeeded, the wheel turned again. The Religious Settlement of 1559 fixed England as a Protestant country. Catholic priests who entered the realm risked being executed for treason — not strictly for what they believed (heresy), but for owing political loyalty to a foreign power, the Pope.

Students often blur heresy and treason together because both could be punished by death and both featured in the same religious upheavals. They are linked but distinct. Heresy is a crime against religious doctrine — holding beliefs the Church declares wrong. Treason is a crime against political authority — betraying loyalty to the monarch. Mary I burnt Protestants for heresy. Elizabeth I executed Catholic priests for treason. Examiners reward students who keep the two terms separate while showing how the Tudors used both to police religious change.

Vagabondage: Criminalising the Wandering Poor

In the early sixteenth century, England’s population grew rapidly while wages stagnated. The dissolution of the monasteries (1536–41) closed the largest providers of poor relief almost overnight. The ‘enclosure’ of common land for sheep farming pushed peasants off ancestral plots. The result was a sharp increase in homeless, jobless people travelling the roads in search of work.

Tudor authorities saw this not as poverty but as a criminal problem. The 1547 Vagrancy Act ordered that any sturdy beggar — a healthy person without work or settled home — could be branded with a ‘V’ on the chest and enslaved for two years on a first offence. A second offence meant death. The law lumped together the genuinely unfortunate and the small minority of professional thieves, treating both as a public danger.

The 1601 Poor Law took a more careful approach. It distinguished between the ‘impotent poor’ — the elderly, the sick, orphaned children — who deserved parish relief, and the ‘sturdy beggars’ or able-bodied poor, who were to be put to work or punished. The split between deserving and undeserving poor would shape English social policy for the next 300 years.

Students often assume that wandering and begging were always criminal. They were not. In the medieval period, wandering pilgrims, journeymen and even beggars at monastery gates were a normal part of life. Vagabondage became a crime in the sixteenth century because economic and religious change — population growth, enclosure, the closure of the monasteries — produced more wanderers than the system could absorb. The state responded by re-classifying their movement as crime. Same behaviour; new law. Examiners reward students who explain that vagrancy was a redefinition of crime, not a new behaviour.

Witchcraft: Why Prosecutions Surged

The first English Witchcraft Act was passed in 1542 under Henry VIII. It made witchcraft a felony — a capital crime tried in the king’s courts rather than the Church courts. Further Acts in 1563 (under Elizabeth I) and 1604 (under James I) tightened the law and increased the penalties.

Several factors drove the surge in prosecutions. Religious anxiety after the Reformation: Protestants and Catholics each suspected the other’s use of supernatural power. Fear of social disorder: a wandering poor and a series of bad harvests in the late sixteenth century created scapegoats. The printing press: cheap pamphlets spread sensational stories of witches who killed cattle, made men impotent, and raised storms. James I’s personal interest: his book Daemonologie (1597) treated witchcraft as a real and pressing danger. Most accused witches were poor, elderly, single women — the people most easily suspected by their neighbours.

In England, witches were typically hanged rather than burnt — burning was reserved for heresy. The largest concentrated witch-hunt would come during the chaos of the Civil War, in the East Anglia hunts of 1645–47 led by Matthew Hopkins (a later lesson). Witchcraft prosecutions wound down in the late seventeenth century as scepticism grew among judges, and the law was finally repealed in 1736.

Continuity: The Old System Still Worked

Alongside these new crimes, much of the older system continued. Tithings and the hue and cry persisted in many villages. Parish constables remained the day-to-day enforcers. In towns, paid watchmen patrolled the streets after dark, calling out the hour and warning of fires — the closest thing to a town police force, but unarmed and often elderly. Royal courts still handled serious offences; Church courts still handled moral cases. What had changed was the menu of crimes, not the basic machinery for trying them.

Key Fact

Witchcraft was made a capital felony in 1542 and tightened by Acts in 1563 and 1604. Religious anxiety, economic hardship, the printing press and royal interest (James I’s Daemonologie, 1597) all helped drive prosecutions.

The strongest answers explain that economic and religious upheaval did not invent new behaviour but led the state to re-classify existing behaviour as crime. For a 16-mark judgement question, weigh up multiple factors (religion, economy, monarchs, technology like the printing press) and reach a substantiated overall judgement signposted in the introduction. Use period vocabulary throughout (vagabondage, heresy, treason, sturdy beggars, impotent poor, felony, Witchcraft Act) for SPaG marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Heresy and treason were reshaped by the Reformation: Mary I burnt Protestants for heresy; Elizabeth I executed Catholic priests for treason — the two crimes are linked but distinct.
  • Vagabondage was redefined as crime by Tudor law (1547 Vagrancy Act); the 1601 Poor Law later split the wandering poor into ‘impotent’ (deserving) and ‘sturdy beggars’ (undeserving).
  • Witchcraft prosecutions surged after the 1542 Act because of religious anxiety, economic stress, cheap printed pamphlets and royal interest; older systems of policing (tithings, parish constables, town watchmen) carried on alongside.

lessons.title: The Gunpowder Plot and the start of the Bloody Code
lessons.description: How the Gunpowder Plot of 1605 set the tone for an age of harsh deterrent punishment.
lessons.content_html:
Policing the Early Modern Town

By the early seventeenth century, English towns were larger and more crowded than in the medieval period, but the basic system of law enforcement had barely changed. There were still no professional police. In rural parishes, the unpaid parish constable kept order in the same way the medieval tithingman had. In towns, his counterpart was the town watchman, also known as the ‘Charley’ in later years, who patrolled the streets after dark, called the hour and raised the alarm if he saw a fire or disturbance.

Town watchmen were unpaid or low-paid, part-time and often elderly. They carried only a lantern, a staff and a rattle. They were not trained, not professional, and were widely mocked. In serious trouble, the public was still expected to raise the hue and cry, and parish constables were still the day-to-day enforcers. The state did not invent or fund a police force; it relied on the community.

Students sometimes describe town watchmen as the start of professional policing. They were not. Watchmen were unpaid or paid very little, served part-time, were locally appointed and had no training. Their job was to walk a beat at night and call out the hour — not to investigate crime. The first paid, organised force came over a century later, with the Bow Street Runners (1749) and then the Metropolitan Police (1829). Examiners reward students who treat the watch as a community-based, amateur system, not as early professional police.

Punishment: Deterrence and Public Spectacle

Without a professional police force, early modern authorities relied on the threat of harsh, public punishment to deter crime. Corporal punishments — flogging, branding, ear-cropping, the pillory and the stocks — were used for theft, vagabondage and minor disorder. Capital punishment — usually hanging — was used for serious property crime as well as for murder, treason and arson. Burning was reserved for heresy and, until 1790, for women convicted of certain forms of treason.

Crucially, punishments were carried out in public. Tyburn in west London was the country’s most famous execution site, where huge crowds gathered on ‘hanging days’. The point was not just to punish the offender but to make every other observer think twice. This is what historians mean by deterrence in the early modern sense: terrifying spectacle as social control.

A New Punishment: Transportation

From around 1615, a new option began to appear in court records: transportation to the American colonies. Convicts were shipped across the Atlantic to work as indentured labour on plantations. For the state, transportation solved several problems at once: it removed criminals from England, it provided cheap labour for the colonies, and it could be presented as mercy — a life saved instead of taken on the gallows.

Transportation was not soft. Conditions on the Atlantic crossing were dangerous; many died. Indentured labour in colonial Virginia or Maryland was hard, hot work, and few transported convicts ever returned to England. By 1700, perhaps two-thirds of those sentenced to death for property crime had their sentence commuted to transportation instead. The punishment regime was therefore beginning to layer alternatives to execution — though execution itself was still on the menu.

Key Fact

Early modern punishment was deliberately public and harsh: hanging, flogging, branding and the pillory were used to deter crime in the absence of a professional police force. Transportation to the American colonies, formalised from 1615, gave courts a harsh alternative to execution.

The Start of the Bloody Code

From the late seventeenth century onwards, Parliament steadily increased the number of offences that carried the death penalty. The 1723 Black Act alone created roughly fifty new capital offences, mostly aimed at poachers in disguise. By the 1810s, more than 200 different crimes were punishable by death — including stealing goods worth more than five shillings, cutting down a young tree, or being out at night with a blackened face. This system became known as the Bloody Code.

The Bloody Code was driven by fear of crime, by the absence of an effective police force, and above all by the wish to protect property. Parliament was dominated by landowners; capital punishment was their main tool against the poor. In practice, however, juries and judges often refused to convict, or commuted death sentences to transportation or pardon. The law on paper was savage; enforcement was uneven.

The Bloody Code is sometimes described as a purely eighteenth-century phenomenon. It is more accurate to say its growth began in the late seventeenth century — the law-making boom of the 1670s and 1680s laid the groundwork — and accelerated rapidly through the eighteenth, peaking in the early nineteenth century before being dismantled by Robert Peel in the 1820s. Examiners reward students who can place the Bloody Code as a long process of expansion (c1688–1820s) rather than a single moment.

Case Study: The Gunpowder Plot, 1605

The most famous early modern treason case began at midnight on 5 November 1605. Acting on a tip-off, royal officials searched the cellars beneath the House of Lords and arrested Guy Fawkes, who was guarding 36 barrels of gunpowder. The plotters, led by Robert Catesby, were a group of English Catholics. Frustrated by James I’s refusal to grant Catholics greater toleration, they intended to blow up the king, his ministers and most of Parliament at the State Opening, then place a Catholic monarch on the throne.

An anonymous letter to a Catholic peer, Lord Monteagle, warned him to stay away. Robert Cecil, James I’s chief minister, used the warning to set the trap. Most of the plotters were either killed resisting arrest at Holbeche House or, like Fawkes, captured and brought to London. Fawkes was tortured on the rack until he gave up the names of his fellow conspirators — one of the few cases of legal torture in English history, used here under royal warrant because of the scale of the threat.

Trial, Punishment and the Treason Spectacle

In January 1606 the surviving plotters were tried for high treason at Westminster Hall. The verdict was never in doubt. They were sentenced to be hanged, drawn and quartered — dragged through the streets on a hurdle, hanged until almost dead, cut down, disembowelled, and then cut into four pieces. The body parts were displayed at city gates and on London Bridge as a permanent warning.

The treason punishment was deliberately more elaborate than ordinary capital punishment because the offence was understood as an attack on the king himself, who in early modern theory ruled by divine right. Punishment for ordinary murder or theft was simply hanging. The Gunpowder Plotters were therefore made into a public spectacle precisely because they had attacked the political and religious order — a reminder of how punishment in this period worked as theatre as well as justice.

Key Fact

The Gunpowder Plotters were hanged, drawn and quartered in January 1606. The treason punishment was deliberately more brutal than ordinary capital punishment because treason was treated as an attack on the king and on God’s appointed political order.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark ‘Explain Why’ question on the importance of the Gunpowder Plot, do not just narrate what happened. Explain why the punishment was so spectacular — the Plot was treason, not ordinary murder, so the state used the most elaborate available punishment to defend the divine right of kings. For a 16-mark ‘Make and Defend a Judgement’ on early modern punishment, weigh deterrence against other purposes (retribution, removing offenders from society via transportation) and signpost your judgement in the introduction. Use period vocabulary throughout (Bloody Code, transportation, town watchmen, hanged drawn and quartered, treason, deterrence) for SPaG marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Early modern policing was still community-based: parish constables in villages and unpaid town watchmen at night — amateur, unarmed and underfunded, not professional police.
  • Punishment relied on public spectacle and deterrence: hanging at Tyburn, flogging, branding and the pillory; transportation to the American colonies, formalised from 1615, gave courts a harsh alternative to execution.
  • The Gunpowder Plot of 1605 ended in the most elaborate punishment available — hanged, drawn and quartered — because treason was treated as an attack on the divine right of kings; this case helped set the tone for the Bloody Code that followed.

lessons.title: Matthew Hopkins and the witch-hunts of 1645–47
lessons.description: Why East Anglia hunted ‘witches’ in the chaos of the Civil War, and how it ended.
lessons.content_html:
A Country at War

In 1645 England was midway through the Civil War between King Charles I and Parliament. Local government was shaken; many Justices of the Peace had been driven from their posts; ordinary travel was disrupted by armies marching, requisitioning food and pressing men into service. In the eastern counties — Essex, Suffolk, Norfolk and Cambridgeshire — Parliament’s authority was strongest, and the local population was overwhelmingly Puritan. It was in this combustible mixture — war, weakened authority, hardline Protestant belief — that the largest English witch-hunt of the early modern period broke out.

Witchcraft itself had been a capital crime in England since the 1542 Witchcraft Act, with stiffer Acts following in 1563 and 1604. James I’s own book Daemonologie (1597) treated witches as a real and active threat, ordered by the Devil. By the 1640s the legal framework, the religious anxiety and the cheap printed pamphlet press were all in place. What was missing — until 1645 — was a determined witch-finder willing to travel from village to village.

Key Fact

The 1645–47 witch-hunts were concentrated in East Anglia because three conditions overlapped there: the chaos of the Civil War weakened normal court oversight, Puritan belief was strong, and Matthew Hopkins was a private witch-finder willing to travel across counties for payment.

Matthew Hopkins, ‘Witchfinder General’

Matthew Hopkins was the son of a Suffolk minister, in his mid-twenties, with no formal legal or religious training. From the spring of 1645 he and his colleague John Stearne began travelling the towns of Essex, Suffolk, Norfolk and Cambridgeshire, offering their services as witch-finders to local magistrates and town corporations. They styled themselves ‘Witchfinder General’, but this was a self-given title, not an official appointment. No king and no Parliament ever named Hopkins to any post.

Hopkins was paid by the towns that hired him, sometimes well over £20 per visit — many times a labourer’s annual wage. The economic incentive was therefore considerable: the more ‘witches’ were found, the more towns paid. In just over two years Hopkins and Stearne were responsible for the prosecution of around 250 women and men, of whom roughly 100 were executed by hanging. This was more witchcraft executions than England had seen in the whole previous century.

Students often describe Hopkins as if he held a royal or parliamentary commission. He did not. The title ‘Witchfinder General’ was Hopkins’s own invention. He worked as a private contractor, paid by individual towns and sometimes by Justices of the Peace. The fact that he could operate at all reflects how weak central oversight had become during the Civil War. As the war ended and judicial authority was restored, Hopkins’s methods came under sceptical scrutiny and he was driven out of business. Examiners reward students who locate Hopkins in his Civil War context, not as a generic state ‘hunter’.

Methods: Watching, Pricking and the Swimming Test

Hopkins’s methods were designed to extract a confession or to manufacture ‘evidence’ that a jury would accept. Three were especially common. The first was watching: a suspect was tied cross-legged on a stool and kept awake for several days while observers watched for the arrival of an ‘imp’ or familiar (a small animal believed to be the Devil’s servant). Sleep deprivation eroded resistance and produced confessions that satisfied the court.

The second was pricking. Witch-finders pushed pins into moles, scars or birthmarks on the suspect’s body looking for the Devil’s mark — a spot that supposedly felt no pain or did not bleed. Some witch-finders used pins with retractable tips that gave the appearance of painless prodding. The third was the swimming test: a suspect was tied with the right thumb to the left big toe and dropped into water. Floating was guilt (the water rejected the witch); sinking was innocence (sometimes too late). All three methods were defended at the time by Hopkins and Stearne in printed books, but were attacked even by contemporaries as unreliable.

A common error is to picture English witches dying at the stake. They did not. In England, witches convicted under the 1542, 1563 and 1604 Acts were hanged like other felons. Burning was reserved for heresy and for women guilty of certain forms of treason. It was Scotland and Continental Europe that burnt witches. Examiners reward students who get this exactly right: in England, hanging; on the Continent and in Scotland, burning. The two systems were genuinely different.

Why the Hunts Targeted Poor, Older Women

Most of the accused were women, most over fifty, and most poor — widows or single women living alone, often dependent on their neighbours’ charity. Several factors converged on this group. Religious belief blamed the Devil for misfortune, and women were widely regarded by Puritan ministers as more open to his temptation. Economic stress meant villagers resented the demands of poor neighbours; refusing alms and then suffering misfortune (a sick child, dead cattle) made it tempting to blame the woman one had refused.

The printing press amplified all of this. Cheap pamphlets — sometimes printed within days of a trial — carried sensational stories of witches who killed cattle, raised storms or made men impotent. A villager who never met a witch could buy a pamphlet describing one. By 1645 there was a ready-made template that fed into accusations and shaped what magistrates expected to find.

Why the Hunts Ended

By 1647 the hunts were collapsing. Three reasons stand out. First, cost: towns balked at the bills Hopkins ran up — food, lodging, fees and the expense of trials. Second, scepticism: educated observers, including the minister John Gaule of Great Staughton, denounced Hopkins’s methods in print. Gaule’s 1646 sermons argued that watching, pricking and swimming proved nothing in law and that anyone could be made to confess by enough sleep deprivation. Third, the personal collapse of Hopkins himself, who was ill and died in 1647, probably of tuberculosis, soon after publishing The Discovery of Witches.

After 1647 English witchcraft prosecutions declined sharply, although the law remained on the statute book. By the late seventeenth century, judges routinely refused to convict on the kinds of evidence Hopkins had produced. The Witchcraft Act was finally repealed in 1736 and replaced with a new Act that punished those claiming to be witches as fraudsters, not capital criminals. Witchcraft was no longer regarded as a real crime in English law.

Key Fact

The 1645–47 hunts produced around 100 hangings — more than England had seen in the previous century. They ended because of cost, growing legal scepticism (notably John Gaule’s 1646 sermons) and the death of Matthew Hopkins himself in 1647.

For a 16-mark ‘Make and Defend a Judgement’ (with SPaG), weigh causes against each other — was the Civil War the most important factor, or was Hopkins himself? Use period vocabulary throughout (witchfinder, Puritan, swimming test, pricking, watching, pamphlet, Demonologie) for SPaG marks. Avoid period-vague words like ‘back then’.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The 1645–47 witch-hunts were the largest in English history, concentrated in East Anglia because the Civil War weakened local courts, Puritan belief was strong and Matthew Hopkins operated as a paid private witch-finder — not as a state official.
  • Hopkins’s methods (watching, pricking, the swimming test) produced around 250 prosecutions and roughly 100 hangings. Convicted witches in England were hanged, not burnt; burning was reserved for heresy.
  • The hunts ended in 1647 because of cost, growing legal scepticism (notably John Gaule’s sermons) and Hopkins’s own death; the Witchcraft Act was finally repealed in 1736.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the witch-hunts of 1645–47 happened in East Anglia.
practice_questions.marks:

Indicative content:

practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement (with SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 16 marks for the historical content, plus up to 4 SPaG marks for accuracy and use of period-specific vocabulary.

Indicative content — arguments supporting the Civil War as the main reason:
• The war (1642–46) disrupted local government in the eastern counties; Justices of the Peace had been removed and judicial oversight was at a low point precisely when Hopkins began operating.
• Armies marching, requisitioning food and pressing men into service produced economic stress and broken communities — the conditions in which scapegoats are most easily found.
• Hopkins’s ability to claim large fees from each town reflects the weakness of central oversight, which would normally have questioned such expenses.

Indicative content — arguments against (other factors):
• East Anglia’s Puritan culture predated the war and provided the religious framework that made witchcraft credible — especially James I’s Demonologie (1597).
• Matthew Hopkins as a determined private witch-finder was the proximate cause; without his energy and willingness to travel, the legal framework would have lain unused.
• The printing press distributed pamphlets that gave villagers a ready-made template for accusations — a long-running cause, not a wartime one.
• Economic stress and bad harvests in the 1640s produced resentment of poor neighbours and made older, poorer women particularly vulnerable to accusation.
• The end of the hunts in 1647 followed the death of Hopkins, the spread of legal scepticism (Gaule’s sermons) and rising costs — not the end of the war alone — suggesting Hopkins himself mattered as much as the war.

Mastering: Sustained, well-supported argument that weighs the Civil War against at least one other factor, uses accurate period vocabulary, and reaches a clear, justified judgement signposted in the introduction and conclusion.
Secure: Both sides considered with relevant detail; judgement is present but less consistently developed.
Developing: One side developed more than the other; judgement asserted rather than defended.
Emerging: Limited argument with little period detail; no clear judgement.

SPaG (4 marks): Accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar with consistent use of subject-specific historical terminology (witchfinder, Puritan, pamphlet, swimming test, pricking, watching, Demonologie).

lessons.title: Eighteenth- and nineteenth-century crime: highwaymen, smugglers and protest
lessons.description: Highway robbery, smuggling and the Tolpuddle Martyrs — new crimes for industrial Britain.
lessons.content_html:
A Society in Transformation

Between c1700 and c1900 Britain changed beyond recognition. The population roughly quadrupled. The Industrial Revolution drew millions from countryside to factory towns. Roads were turnpiked, canals cut, and from the 1830s railways began to bind the country into a single national market. New wealth in banks and warehouses created new things to steal; new kinds of work created new ways to protest. Crimes did not vanish — theft and assault continued — but new categories of crime appeared, and old ones (such as the witchcraft prosecutions abolished in 1736) faded away. This lesson examines three: highway robbery, smuggling, and the criminalisation of trade-union activity that produced the Tolpuddle Martyrs.

Highway Robbery: Rise and Fall

Highway robbery peaked in the early eighteenth century. Long stretches of unlit road between towns gave armed men on horseback the chance to stop coaches at pistol point and demand purses, watches and jewellery. The most famous — Dick Turpin, hanged at York in 1739 — was in life a violent burglar and horse thief; the romantic legend of the ‘gentleman of the road’ was largely a Victorian invention.

By the 1830s and 1840s highway robbery had collapsed as a serious problem. Several changes explain this. Turnpike trusts produced better-lit, busier roads, with more passing traffic and toll-keepers. Banking reforms, especially the spread of bank notes and cheques in the early 1800s, meant travellers carried less gold and silver. Mounted patrols, set up by the Bow Street Runners under the Fielding brothers, swept the main roads out of London. Above all, railways — from the 1830s — allowed long-distance travellers to move faster than any horse, and entirely off the road network. The conditions that had made highway robbery possible were systematically dismantled.

Students who lean on Victorian novels often glamorise highwaymen as polite, well-dressed robbers who only stole from the rich. The reality was harsher. Most highwaymen were violent: they threatened, beat and sometimes killed their victims. Dick Turpin himself was a member of the Essex Gang of farm-burglars who tortured householders to find hidden money — not a romantic hero. The legend grew after his execution because cheap printed broadsides made ‘gentleman of the road’ ballads sell. Examiners reward students who treat highway robbery as a serious property crime, not as folklore.

Smuggling and Social Crime

Smuggling grew rapidly in the eighteenth century because the government raised customs duties on tea, brandy, lace and tobacco to fund foreign wars. By the 1780s smuggled goods were so common in coastal counties — Cornwall, Sussex, Kent — that local communities cooperated openly with the gangs that landed them. Whole villages benefited: tea drunk in a Cornish kitchen had often crossed the beach the night before. The state regarded smuggling as a serious crime; many local people regarded it as a tolerable way of dodging unfair taxation.

Historians describe this as social crime — crime in law that is accepted, or even popular, in the wider community. Poaching of game on landowners’ estates was social crime in the same sense: the 1723 Black Act made poaching of deer or game while disguised a capital offence, but most rural villagers regarded a snared rabbit as legitimate winter food. Smuggling declined sharply after the 1840s, when free-trade reforms (especially under William Gladstone) cut customs duties on imported goods. With the profit margin gone, the trade collapsed.

Key Fact

Smuggling and poaching were ‘social crimes’: serious in law but tolerated or supported by local communities. Smuggling thrived because eighteenth-century customs duties were high; it collapsed after free-trade reforms in the 1840s removed the profit.

The 1736 Witchcraft Act: Crime Re-defined

A different kind of change is illustrated by the end of witchcraft prosecutions. The 1736 Witchcraft Act repealed the older 1604 Act and re-defined the offence: it was now a crime to claim magical powers as a fraudster, not to actually be a witch. By 1736, judges in central courts had largely stopped accepting the kind of evidence Hopkins had relied on, and educated opinion regarded witchcraft prosecutions as embarrassing. The Witchcraft Act 1736 thus marks a turning point — not a change in human behaviour but a change in what the state would call a crime. By 1900 even the new Act was being used only against fortune-tellers and was finally repealed in 1951.

Students often assume that the 1736 Act marked a moment when British people, top and bottom of society, stopped believing in witches. The reality is more uneven. Educated judges and lawyers had grown sceptical decades earlier. Belief at village level lasted much longer; informal accusations and even attacks on supposed witches continued in some areas into the early nineteenth century. The 1736 Act reflected a shift in legal opinion among the elite, not in popular belief. Examiners reward students who can explain that legal change preceded popular change.

Trade Unions and the 1797 Unlawful Oaths Act

The 1799 and 1800 Combination Acts banned workers from combining to demand higher wages. They were repealed in 1824, partly because Parliament accepted that combinations were inevitable in industrial society. After 1824 trade unions were therefore legal in Britain. Yet they remained politically suspect, especially after the 1832 Reform Act had given the vote to middle-class men but not to working-class men. Local landowners and magistrates feared that unionised farm labourers would demand higher wages and refuse to work; in 1832 the Whig government of Lord Melbourne was already alarmed by rural unrest.

The Tolpuddle Martyrs, 1834

In the village of Tolpuddle in Dorset, six farm labourers led by George Loveless agreed in 1834 to form a ‘Friendly Society of Agricultural Labourers’. Their aim was to keep wages from being cut from seven shillings a week to six. As part of joining, members swore a secret oath of loyalty to one another. The local landowner James Frampton denounced them to the government. They were arrested under the Unlawful Oaths Act of 1797 — an obscure law originally aimed at naval mutineers — not for forming a union, which was already legal.

At their trial in March 1834, the six men were sentenced to seven years’ transportation to Australia. They became known as the Tolpuddle Martyrs. The harshness of the sentence triggered a national protest campaign: a London demonstration in April 1834 was reported as 100,000 strong, and a petition gathered 800,000 signatures. The pressure paid off. In 1836 the men were granted a free pardon by the new Whig government, and most returned to Britain by 1838. The case became a landmark in trade-union history: not because it expanded the law — the prosecution had been an old-law manoeuvre — but because it galvanised public sympathy and made the labour movement politically respectable.

Key Fact

Trade unions had been legal since 1824. The Tolpuddle Martyrs were therefore prosecuted under an obscure 1797 Unlawful Oaths Act, not for forming a union. They were sentenced to seven years’ transportation in 1834 and pardoned in 1836 after a national protest campaign.

What Changed, and Why

Across this period, the underlying picture is the same: definitions of crime change as society’s priorities change. Highway robbery declined because better roads, banking reform and railways made it impractical, not because moral attitudes against robbery changed. Smuggling declined because lower customs duties removed the profit, not because villagers suddenly judged it immoral. Witchcraft was decriminalised because educated legal opinion shifted; popular belief lagged behind. Trade-union activity moved from secrecy and prosecution (1797–1834) to public respectability (after 1836) because the politics of organised labour, not the law itself, changed. The list of crimes is always partly a portrait of who holds power.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For a 4-mark ‘Describe Two Features’ question on the Tolpuddle Martyrs, do not muddle the law: they were charged under the 1797 Unlawful Oaths Act, not for forming a union (legal since 1824). For a 16-mark ‘Make and Defend a Judgement’ on changing definitions of crime, weigh different factors (technology, the economy, attitudes, government) and reach a substantiated overall judgement signposted in the introduction. For an 8-mark ‘Explain the Importance’ question on the Tolpuddle Martyrs, focus on consequences — the 800,000-signature petition and 1836 pardon, and the boost to public acceptance of organised labour. Use period vocabulary throughout (transportation, social crime, Bloody Code, Combination Acts, friendly society) for SPaG marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Highway robbery and smuggling thrived in the eighteenth century but collapsed in the nineteenth: highway robbery undermined by turnpikes, banking reform and railways; smuggling killed off by free-trade reforms in the 1840s.
  • Witchcraft prosecutions ended with the 1736 Witchcraft Act, which redefined witchcraft as fraud rather than a real crime; this was a change in legal opinion among the elite, not in popular belief.
  • The Tolpuddle Martyrs (1834) were transported under an obscure 1797 Unlawful Oaths Act — not for forming a union (legal since 1824). The 1836 pardon followed a national protest of around 800,000 signatures and helped legitimise the trade-union movement.

• It led directly to the free pardon in 1836 and the Martyrs’ return by 1838 — an early example of mass campaigning forcing the government to overturn a court sentence.
• It legitimised the labour movement, making trade-union activity more publicly respectable in Victorian Britain.
• It illustrates the wider point that definitions of crime change as politics changes — what was prosecuted in 1834 was politically unthinkable a generation later.

lessons.title: Robert Peel and the birth of the Metropolitan Police
lessons.description: From the Bow Street Runners to Peel’s bobbies: building a professional police force.
lessons.content_html:
A Police Crisis

By 1820 London was the largest city in the world. Its population had passed one million; its docks handled more cargo than any other port; its streets were crowded with horses, traders and migrants. But the system of policing was almost unchanged from Tudor times. Each parish appointed unpaid parish constables and night watchmen — sometimes called ‘Charlies’. They were unpaid or paid very little, served part-time, and were widely mocked as old, drunk or asleep on duty.

The army filled the gap when riots broke out, but soldiers were poorly suited to civilian crowd control. The Peterloo Massacre of 1819 — in which yeomanry cavalry killed eighteen protestors at a peaceful Manchester rally — showed the political cost of using the army for policing. Yet calls for a new police force met long-standing public suspicion. Britons feared a uniformed force would resemble the secret police of revolutionary France: a tool of state spying, not local justice. Reform therefore had to be designed to reassure the public, not just to catch criminals.

The Bow Street Runners: A First Attempt

The first organised paid policing in London predated 1829 by eighty years. Henry Fielding, the novelist and London magistrate, recruited a small group of men in 1749 to investigate crime from his Bow Street courtroom. They became known as the Bow Street Runners. Fielding’s blind half-brother John Fielding — said to be able to recognise 3,000 criminals by their voices — took over the Bow Street court after Henry’s death and expanded the operation. From 1763 a mounted Horse Patrol swept the main roads out of London.

The Runners were a success on their own terms but a small one: never more than a few dozen men, paid partly by reward, working only out of central London. They had no national reach and no presence in the rapidly growing industrial cities. They were absorbed into the Metropolitan Police in 1839. Their importance is that they proved a paid, organised force could work and be politically tolerable — an example for the much larger reform that followed.

Students often claim that Robert Peel invented organised policing in 1829. He did not. Tithings, parish constables and night watchmen had policed England for nearly a thousand years. The Bow Street Runners had been an organised, paid force in London since 1749. What Peel did was professionalise existing efforts and unify them under a single command, with full-time pay, uniform and beats. Calling 1829 the start of policing misses the eighty years of Bow Street experience that made it possible. Examiners reward students who place Peel as a continuity-and-change figure, not a sole inventor.

Robert Peel as Home Secretary

Robert Peel became Home Secretary in 1822. He inherited the Bloody Code in its full form — over 200 capital offences. Between 1823 and 1827 he led a major penal reform, repealing several hundred capital statutes and reducing the offences for which one could be hanged. Death remained on the books for murder and treason, but ordinary property crime was now mostly punishable by transportation or prison. This reform mattered because Peel was preparing the ground for a police force: harsh laws were more enforceable when paired with proportionate punishment.

In 1829 Peel introduced the Metropolitan Police Act. The Act created a single force for the London area (excluding the City of London, which kept its own force). Headquarters were at Scotland Yard, on Whitehall Place; the back entrance, which became the public face of the force, gave it its informal name. The first commissioners were Sir Charles Rowan and Sir Richard Mayne, who together drafted the rules of conduct emphasising prevention, civility and the consent of the governed.

Peelers, Bobbies and Beat Patrols

The new police were nicknamed ‘Peelers’ or ‘bobbies’, both after their founder. Their design was deliberately reassuring. Officers wore a blue coat and top hat — not military red. They carried only a wooden truncheon and a rattle, not a firearm. They worked fixed beats: each constable patrolled a defined route on foot, day or night, so the public knew which officer to expect and the officer learned the people. The aim was prevention through visible, regular presence, not investigation after the fact.

Recruitment standards were strict by the standards of the day. Recruits had to be under 35, at least 5 feet 7 inches tall, literate and of good character. They were full-time and salaried — not paid by reward. The first three years saw heavy turnover — many recruits were dismissed for drunkenness — but by the mid-1830s a stable corps of around 3,000 officers was in place.

Key Fact

Peel’s force was deliberately civilian: blue coat (not red), wooden truncheon (not firearm), fixed foot beats and a focus on prevention. The 1829 Metropolitan Police Act created the force; Sir Robert Peel was Home Secretary and Sir Richard Mayne and Sir Charles Rowan were the first commissioners.

It is tempting to imagine the new police were welcomed at once. They were not. Many Londoners ridiculed them as ‘raw lobsters’ and ‘blue plagues’. There were violent attacks: PC Robert Culley was killed at a riot in Coldbath Fields, Clerkenwell in 1833 and a coroner’s jury initially returned a verdict of ‘justifiable homicide’. Public acceptance came only over the 1830s and 1840s, helped by visible reductions in crime, by the bobby’s unarmed civility and by the sheer fact of seeing the same officer on the same beat every day. Examiners reward students who can show that public consent was earned, not given.

Spreading the Model: County Forces and CID

The Met covered only the London area. Outside London, parishes still relied on their old constables. Two Acts changed that. The 1839 County Police Act gave magistrates the option of setting up a paid county force, modelled on the Met. Many counties did so; many did not, on grounds of cost. The 1856 County and Borough Police Act made paid forces compulsory in every county and borough. By the late 1850s, every part of England and Wales had a Peel-style police force.

Detective work followed. The 1842 Detective Branch was a small unit of plain-clothes officers based at Scotland Yard. They handled serious crime that the uniformed beats could not pursue. In 1878, after a corruption scandal, the Branch was reorganised and renamed the Criminal Investigation Department (CID), with stricter recruitment and supervision. By the 1880s CID had several hundred officers and was the model copied by other forces. It would soon be tested by the Whitechapel murders of 1888 — the subject of this unit’s historic environment study.

Key Fact

Key dates: 1749 Bow Street Runners; 1829 Metropolitan Police Act; 1839 County Police Act (optional county forces); 1842 Detective Branch; 1856 County and Borough Police Act (compulsory forces nationwide); 1878 CID created.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark ‘Explain the Importance’ question on the 1829 Metropolitan Police Act, do not just describe the new force. Explain its consequences — the model spread to counties (1839 and 1856 Acts), the principle of unarmed civilian policing took root, and the foundation was laid for CID in 1878. For a 16-mark ‘Make and Defend a Judgement (with SPaG)’ question on Peel, weigh his role against earlier developments (parish constables, the Bow Street Runners) and reach a substantiated overall judgement. Use period vocabulary throughout (parish constable, watchman, beat, peeler, bobby, truncheon, Scotland Yard, Detective Branch, CID) for SPaG marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Pre-1829 policing was mostly amateur: parish constables and night watchmen, with the Bow Street Runners (1749) the only paid force. The Peterloo Massacre showed the army was not a workable substitute.
  • Peel professionalised existing efforts: the 1829 Metropolitan Police Act created a unified, salaried, uniformed force based at Scotland Yard, deliberately unarmed and civilian to win public consent over time.
  • The model spread nationally with the 1839 and 1856 County Police Acts; the Detective Branch (1842) became CID in 1878 — the body that would lead the Whitechapel investigation a decade later.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Robert Peel introduced the Metropolitan Police in 1829.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of two or more reasons, supported by accurate detail.

Indicative content:
• London’s population had passed a million by 1820 and old systems of unpaid parish constables and watchmen could no longer cope with urban crime.
• Recent disturbances — including the 1819 Peterloo Massacre, where the army had killed eighteen protestors — showed that using soldiers for crowd control was politically unacceptable.
• The Bow Street Runners had proved since 1749 that a paid, organised force could work, but they were small and confined to central London.
• Peel had already begun reforming the Bloody Code (1823–27); harsh laws were more enforceable when paired with proportionate punishment, which required a police force to catch the people who would now be punished by prison or transportation rather than execution.
• Public anxiety about French-style state policing had to be addressed by a force that was uniformed, civilian and unarmed — the design Peel produced.

Mastering: Sustained explanation of at least two reasons with specific detail (population, Peterloo, Bow Street, penal reform) and explicit links to the question.
Secure: Two reasons explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the new force without explaining why.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the 1829 Metropolitan Police Act.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of the Act, supported by accurate detail.

Indicative content:
• It established the first uniformed, salaried, professional police force for the London area, with headquarters at Scotland Yard.
• It set the template — civilian uniform, unarmed beat patrol, focus on prevention — that the 1839 and 1856 County Police Acts spread across England and Wales.
• It made detective work possible at scale: the Detective Branch (1842) and the CID (1878) were direct successors of Peel’s force.
• It established the principle of policing by consent — an unarmed officer walking a known beat — that became central to British attitudes to the police.
• It allowed Peel’s parallel reforms of the Bloody Code to work, since proportionate punishment required reliable detection.

Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons named with limited detail.

practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement (with SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 16 marks for the historical content, plus up to 4 SPaG marks for accuracy and use of period-specific vocabulary.

Indicative content — arguments supporting Peel as the most important reason:
• Peel as Home Secretary delivered the 1829 Metropolitan Police Act, creating the first unified, salaried, uniformed force.
• Peel had already reformed the Bloody Code (1823–27), so a police force could be paired with proportionate punishment — the two reforms were a single project.
• Peel personally drafted the principles of consent and prevention, with Rowan and Mayne, that defined British policing.
• His name remained attached to the force (‘Peelers’, ‘bobbies’) and his model was adopted by every force created after him.

Indicative content — arguments against (other factors mattered as much or more):
• Henry and John Fielding had created the Bow Street Runners (1749) and the Horse Patrol (1763), proving that paid policing could work; without this eighty-year experience the Met would not have been politically possible.
• The growth of London’s population past a million, plus rapid industrialisation in cities like Manchester and Birmingham, made reform inevitable; Peel’s timing reflected demographic pressure as much as personal initiative.
• The Peterloo Massacre (1819) discredited the army for civilian policing and forced reform; the political climate, not Peel alone, drove the change.
• The 1839 and 1856 County Police Acts — passed under different governments — spread the model nationally; Peel did not personally extend the Met beyond London.
• CID (1878), the most important nineteenth-century development for serious crime, came thirty years after Peel’s death and was driven by scandal and necessity, not by his planning.

Mastering: Sustained, well-supported argument that weighs Peel against at least one other factor, uses accurate period vocabulary, and reaches a clear, justified judgement signposted in the introduction and conclusion.
Secure: Both sides considered with relevant detail; judgement is present but less consistently developed.
Developing: One side developed more than the other; judgement asserted rather than defended.
Emerging: Limited argument with little period detail; no clear judgement.

SPaG (4 marks): Accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar with consistent use of subject-specific historical terminology (parish constable, watchman, beat constable, peeler, bobby, Scotland Yard, Detective Branch, CID).
