practice_questions.text:
Explain why investigating the Whitechapel murders was so difficult for the police in autumn 1888.

You may use the following in your answer:
• detective methods of the period
• cooperation between police forces.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 12 marks for an answer that explicitly links named local detail to wider contextual factors of late-Victorian policing. Indicative content — specifics: • Detective methods limited to witness statements, sketches, crime-scene photography (Mitre Square) and post-mortems by surgeons such as Thomas Bond; no fingerprinting, no blood-typing, no central suspect database. • The Met/City boundary at Aldgate created procedural problems — the ‘double event’ on 30 September involved both forces, and Sir Charles Warren’s erasure of the Goulston Street graffito was made without consulting the City Police. • Press interference: the ‘Dear Boss’ letter (almost certainly a journalist’s hoax) named the killer in every paper before police could investigate; this drowned the case in tips and false leads. • The lodging-house economy and lack of guest registers meant witnesses moved frequently and could be untraceable a week later. Indicative content — wider contextual factors: • The CID was small and only ten years old (founded 1878); detective expertise was concentrated at Scotland Yard, not spread across H Division. • Public trust in the Met under Sir Charles Warren had already been damaged by Bloody Sunday in November 1887, making witnesses cautious of cooperating. • The mass press of 1888 was new in scale — The Star, Pall Mall Gazette, Punch all ran the case daily — and shaped public expectation of an arrest faster than any Victorian force could realistically deliver. • The Whitechapel Vigilance Committee’s civilian patrols, while well-intentioned, sometimes complicated police timelines by adding amateur witnesses to the mix. Mastering: Sustained explanation that links named specifics (Goulston Street, Met/City split, ‘Dear Boss’, lodging-house anonymity) to at least two wider contextual factors (CID size, post-Bloody-Sunday distrust, the mass press), with a clear conclusion. Secure: Specifics linked to one wider factor, with a developed explanation. Developing: Specifics described, but the link to wider context is asserted rather than developed. Emerging: Description of events without explicit links to wider context.

practice_questions.text:
‘The Whitechapel Vigilance Committee was the most significant non-police response to the Ripper murders.’

How far do you agree? Explain your answer.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the Whitechapel Vigilance Committee

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement (with SPaG)
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 16 marks for the historical content, plus up to 4 SPaG marks for accuracy and use of period-specific vocabulary. Indicative content — arguments supporting the Vigilance Committee as most significant: • Formed in September 1888 under George Lusk after the Chapman murder; demonstrates organised civil society stepping in. • Organised civilian patrols of the rookeries, hired private detectives and lobbied for a public reward — concrete actions on the ground. • Received the ‘From Hell’ letter and half a kidney on 16 October 1888 — a genuine piece of evidence that the Committee handled and forwarded to the Met. • Modelled a template for community policing in poor areas where state policing was perceived to be failing. Indicative content — arguments against (other significant responses): • Press coverage: The Star, Pall Mall Gazette and Punch shaped public understanding of the murders, named the killer (the ‘Dear Boss’ letter, almost certainly a hoax) and drove the political pressure that brought down Sir Charles Warren on 8 November 1888. • Booth’s 1889 poverty map was a non-police social-investigation response that reframed the slums as a measurable, reform-able problem. • Andrew Mearns’s The Bitter Cry of Outcast London (1883) had already framed the East End for middle-class readers before the murders began, shaping the response when they did. • Reform-minded politicians at the Home Office (Henry Matthews) and individual MPs played a role too, although they refused the public reward Lusk requested. Mastering: Sustained, well-supported argument that weighs the Vigilance Committee against at least two other responses (press, social investigation, political reform), uses accurate period vocabulary and reaches a clear, justified judgement signposted in the introduction and conclusion. Secure: Both sides considered with relevant detail; judgement is present but less consistently developed. Developing: One side developed more than the other; judgement is asserted rather than defended. Emerging: Limited argument with little period detail; no clear judgement. SPaG (4 marks): Accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar with consistent use of subject-specific historical terminology (e.g. canonical five, Vigilance Committee, ‘Dear Boss’, Goulston Street graffito, CID, H Division).
